McCreary County sits in southeastern Kentucky and uses the Kentucky certificate of delinquency system for unpaid real property taxes. That means investors are usually buying tax lien certificates, not tax deeds, at the county clerk sale. This guide explains how McCreary County tax sales work, what the recent county notice showed, how bidding is handled under Kentucky rules, and what investors should check before spending money.

What is McCreary County’s tax sale system?

McCreary County sells certificates of delinquency through the county clerk. In Kentucky, these sales usually begin in mid July and run into the fall, with most counties holding sales from mid July through late August. In plain English, you are buying the tax lien claim tied to unpaid taxes. You do not get the property on sale day. If the owner does not pay later, the certificate holder may enforce the lien through the court process.

Important Details

The table below gives the short version for McCreary County. The county clerk’s recent public notice listed a sale on August 26 at 10:00 AM Eastern Time, with registration due by the close of business on August 15. The county clerk page lists McCreary County in the Eastern Time zone.

Key Takeaways

  • McCreary County sells certificates of delinquency for unpaid property taxes, typically starting in mid-July.
  • Investors buy tax lien certificates, not property on sale day; certificates can yield 1% interest per month.
  • Registration is required before the sale; bidders must follow specific Kentucky rules during the auction process.
  • Due diligence is essential; check property access, ownership history, and the current status of delinquent taxes.
  • Post-sale, investors can buy remaining certificates directly from the county clerk, providing a calmer purchasing experience.

Fun Facts About the County

  • McCreary County had a population of 16,888 at the 2020 Census.
  • Big South Fork National River and Recreation Area reaches into McCreary County and covers about 125,000 acres on the Cumberland Plateau.
  • Daniel Boone National Forest stretches across 21 counties in eastern Kentucky, including land near McCreary County.
  • McCreary County promotes its access to I 75, a rail line, and lower living costs as part of its business pitch.

Attractions & Economic Highlights

  • Attractions: Big South Fork National River and Recreation Area and nearby Daniel Boone National Forest.
  • Transportation: The county promotes access to I 75 and a rail line.
  • Economy: Outdoor travel, small business, local services, and county level business development matter here.
  • Community: Hiking, trail riding, camping, and river based recreation shape local appeal.

Why This County is Ideal for Tax Lien Investors

  • Kentucky tax lien certificates can offer high returns through 1% simple interest per month plus certain allowed fees.
  • McCreary County is a smaller rural market, which can help investors find state tax lien opportunities without major metro competition. This is an inference based on county size and population.
  • Entry costs can be lower than many deed states because buyers purchase the lien claim, not the full property on day one.
  • For patient buyers who want a low risk investment approach, lien certificates can fit better than jumping into full rehab deals. That still depends on strong due diligence.

Auction Process for Tax Lien Sales

McCreary County follows the Kentucky county clerk tax sale system. The county clerk posts the delinquent tax information and a sale notice. Buyers who need state registration must first get their Kentucky certificate. Then they must register with the county clerk, submit their lists, pay fees, and post deposits before the local deadline.

Kentucky does not use a bid down interest auction in this process. Instead, after priority claims are handled, the county uses a random drawing to set buyer order. Then registered buyers choose certificates from the lists they already submitted. The return comes from the lien rules, not from bidding the rate down on sale day.

How the Auction Works

Here is a simple look at how the McCrearyCounty tax lien sale works from notice through post-sale rights.

  1. Review the list

    The county clerk posts the delinquent tax list and notice before the sale. Bills may still drop off if owners pay.

  2. Register before the deadline

    County registration requires the local form, your certificate of registration if needed, your purchase lists, fees, and deposits.

  3. Priority claims go first

    If you already hold a prior year lien on the same property, you may have first priority for the current year certificate.

  4. Random drawing sets order

    The county then uses a random drawing to set the order for remaining certificates.

  5. Buyers select from filed lists

    You can only choose certificates that were on your submitted list. Deposits are credited toward what you buy.

Maximum Potential Returns and Expected Returns on McCreary County Tax Lien Certificates

The main return on a Kentucky certificate of delinquency is 1% simple interest per month on the amount paid to the county clerk. On top of that, the holder may add certain administrative costs and limited pre litigation attorney fees allowed by statute. That means your expected return depends on how long the lien stays unpaid and what costs are recoverable. There is no county auction rate bidding here. Your return follows the Kentucky collection rules after purchase.

Open to All Investors and Foreign Investor Participation

Kentucky’s rules do not frame county tax lien buying as residents only. The regulation defines a “person” broadly to include individuals and business entities. If the buyer meets the registration rules, files the needed paperwork, and is in good standing where required, the buyer may participate. For larger buyers, the state registration step must be completed at least 60 days before purchase.

For foreign or out of state investors, the practical issue is paperwork and compliance. You still need the right entity setup, good records, and the county level registration package. Many remote buyers use local help for title review, occupancy checks, and site photos before they buy. That is not a legal rule. It is just smart practice.

Importance of Due Diligence in McCreary County Tax Lien Investing

What Due Diligence Entails

  • Check the parcel and owner record through county records.
  • Review the delinquent tax listing and confirm the bill is still active before sale time.
  • Study access, land use, flood issues, and physical condition.
  • Budget for legal work if foreclosure becomes necessary.

Risks of Skipping Due Diligence

  • You may buy a lien on land with poor access or weak resale value.
  • The owner may redeem fast, which can shorten your hold period.
  • Court enforcement takes time and money after the one year waiting period.
  • A bad file review can turn a small lien into a slow project.

Buying Over the Counter Liens in McCreary County

How to Purchase OTC Liens

If any certificates remain unsold after the tax sale, Kentucky allows them to be bought later. The manual says remaining certificates may be purchased at any time by a third party after the sale, subject to registration rules and per bill fees. So in McCreary County, ask the clerk whether any post sale certificates are still open.

Benefits of OTC Purchases

OTC buying can be easier because there is no sale room pressure and no random drawing that day. You still need to follow Kentucky rules, but you can review remaining liens more calmly.

Why McCreary County is a Top Choice for Tax Lien Investors

Economic and Tax Advantages

  • Small county size can mean a manageable list for hands on buyers. This is an inference from county population.
  • Kentucky has a uniform county clerk tax lien process.
  • The county markets access to I 75 and rail service.

Real Estate Market Overview

McCreary County is a rural market. That can work well for land focused investors who know how to value access, topography, and exit demand. It is not a place to buy blind. The best deals here usually come from careful file review and realistic resale plans, not from hype. County scale and outdoor appeal can help, but your profit still comes from the numbers.

Conclusion

McCreary County, Kentucky is a tax lien certificate county. The county clerk handles the sale, and Kentucky law sets most of the ground rules. The recent county notice showed a late August sale, 10:00 AM Eastern start time, county clerk registration, and a local deadline before sale day. Buyers earn returns through simple monthly interest and allowed fees, not from bid down interest.

That makes McCreary County a solid fit for investors who like paper backed tax lien positions and who have the patience to follow the Kentucky process from purchase to payoff or enforcement. Just remember that smart investing starts with thorough research. Check every parcel, verify each bill, and plan your exit before you buy.

Pro Tips

  • Focus on parcels with clear access and simple ownership history.
  • Call the clerk before the deadline and confirm deposit rules.
  • Build your list early because buyers can only pick from filed certificates.
  • Treat rural land value with care. Cheap does not always mean easy resale.
  • Ask whether any liens remain after the sale for OTC buying.

FAQs for McCreary County Tax Liens

Do I get the property right away?

No. You buy the lien claim, not the deed.

Can I start foreclosure right after buying?

No. Kentucky has a one year wait before enforcement action.

Can I renovate the property after the sale?

Not unless you later become owner through the legal process.

Are other costs added to the lien?

Yes. Kentucky allows interest and certain fees.

Can I resell my certificate?

Assignments are addressed under Kentucky lien rules and should be reviewed before purchase.
